messages.author: 2ffa956ce2411d70
messages.subject: [ez4r] potential problem with type = 3
parts:
Hi Mike,

I stumbled upon a potential problem with setting the type of the Sums
of Square to 3 in ezANOVA today. (Some background, I got the proofs
for a paper and wanted to recheck everything. As the original analyses
was done in SPSS, I had to use type 3.)
The design is a 2 (between) x 2 x 2 (within) with unequal sample sizes
(27 vs 28).
When running this using ezANOVA I get the exact same results when
setting type to 2 and type to 3. This obviously shouldn't happen (and
doesn't happen in SPSS).

I attach you the file with the data (exp2.RData). The code I am using
is the following:

require(ez)

load("exp2.RData")

type2 <- ezANOVA(exp2, dv = .(value), wid = .(id), within = .(problem,
type), between = .(instruction), detailed = TRUE, type = 2)

type3 <- ezANOVA(exp2, dv = .(value), wid = .(id), within = .(problem,
type), between = .(instruction), detailed = TRUE, type = 3)

all.equal(type2, type3)

[1] TRUE

You can compare this with the results from SPSS. I attach you the same
data in SPSS format and the SPSS syntax as well. As you will see, the
F-values from ez match those from SPSS's type = 2

# get them in R via:
round(type2[["ANOVA"]][["F"]],3)[-1]

# Note that the order is different from SPSS to ez

Sorry, for going on your nerves with this. I hope it is just my fault.
Because, I really like ez and your work. It's the only thing I use for
running ANOVAs in R.

Thank you so much,

Henrik

parts:
Hi Henrick,

Apologies for the delayed reply; you happened to post your email to
the list on the day my first child was born, so my availability has
been rather limited of late!

You've stumbled on a bug that is rather embarrassing for me: one of
the big features introduced in ez3.0 was the ability to specify type=3
in the call to ezANOVA, and yet I appear to have hard-coded all
subsequent calls to car::Anova() with type=2!

Until the next release of ez, you can fix this by grabbing the latest
versions of ezANOVA.R
(https://github.com/mike-lawrence/ez/blob/master/R/ezANOVA.R) and
ez-internal.R (https://github.com/mike-lawrence/ez/blob/master/R/ez-internal.R)
from github then source them after loading up ez the regular way:

library(ez)
source('ezANOVA.R')
source('ez-internal.R')

Cheers,

Mike

messages.author: 2ffa956ce2411d70
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] potential problem with type = 3
parts:
Hi Mike,

thanks for getting back to this issue and providing a fix. With this fix now ez computes type 3 sums. However, there is still an issue that I think is debatable. It relates to the way that ez computes the type 3 SSs in comparison to how SPSS (and probably SAS) do it.

At first, I think it would be great if one could get the same results in R as in SPSS, as SPSS is the de facto standard in our field (i.e., psychology).

What ez now returns as type 3 sum of squares is only identical to the SPSS results for within subjects effects for the highest order interaction, for the lower ones it diverges (sometimes massively).

Takethe example I already presented in my previous mail. There are 2 within subject factors: type with 3 levels and problem (=prob) with 2 levels. Furthermore one between subjects factor (instr) with 2 levels resulting in a: 2 (between) x 3 (within) x 2 (within) so called split-plot ANOVA. The following table (hopefully readable) compares the F-values from both programs. Furthermore, the last column gives the F-values of type 2 SS (they are identical in ez and SPSS):

| Effect          |   F-ez | F-SPSS | same? | Type II |
|-----------------+--------+--------+-------+---------|
| instr           |  0.005 |  0.005 | yes   |   0.005 |
| prob            | 50.871 | 87.128 | no    |  85.653 |
| instr:prob      | 19.782 | 19.782 | yes   |  19.782 |
| type            |  4.624 | 29.319 | no    |  29.433 |
| instr:type      |  3.831 |  3.831 | yes   |   3.831 |
| prob:type       |  1.059 | 63.933 | no    |  64.542 |
| instr:prob:type |  4.845 |  4.845 | yes   |   4.845 |
|-----------------+--------+--------+-------+---------|
(instr = between 2 levels; prob = within 2 levels; type = within 3 levels)

Here one can easily see the differences for lower level interactions and main effects for the type 3 SS. They are huge. Furthermore, the SPSS results for type 2 and type 3 sums are pretty much comparable overall. They differ only slightly. When one looks at this, the type 3 SS don't seem to be so unreasonable at all. (interestingly the results that match between ez and spps are also identical to the type 2 results..)

The differences are probably related to the way which terms are included in computing the type 3 sums. SPSS help says:
"The Type III sum of squares for an effect F can best be described as the sum of squares for F adjusted for effects that do not contain it, and orthogonal to effects (if any) that contain it."

To further nail this down, I tried to get the same results from SPSS that ez returns for the lower terms, but failed to obtain them.

My idea would be, that if one asks for type 3 sums in ez one (at least me) would expect to obtain the results that spss would give for this case. As this is what most people report in their papers if they talk about ANOVAs.

What do you respectively other list members think about that?

Let me finally add two things:

1. All the best to you and your family. It is great to hear that young scientists find the time to start a family.

2. ez is really great. Before knowing and regularly using ez, I always switched back to SPSS just for calculating ANOVAs. Your package made this step obsolete. ez is one of the few packages I use in almost all projects. Thank you for taking your time and producing this for the community.

Best,

Henrik

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] potential problem with type = 3
parts:
I tracked down the difference to 2 sources:

1) ez treats numeric between variables as numeric (thus fitting linear
effects when that variable is involved in an effect) whereas you
probably have told SPSS to treat your numeric variable "instruction"
as categorical. To make R treat "instruction" as categorical, convert
it to a factor.

2) SPSS seems to be set up with sum contrasts by default, whereas R
uses treatment contrasts by default. To make R use sum contrasts by
default, run: options(contrasts=c('contr.sum','contr.poly'))

In future versions of ez I'll provide an easier way to ask for
different contrasts and put some description of SPSS's default
behaviour.
